newsitem.title: UK: TREASURIES CLIMB IN LONDON, NERVOUS AFTER FALL.
newsitem.headline: TREASURIES CLIMB IN LONDON, NERVOUS AFTER FALL.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries firmed on Monday, correcting some of the oversold signs after Friday's sharp drop. But investors were nervous ahead of key U.S. data this week.
"It's a typical Monday, there has been quite a bit of buying coming through," said one trader at a Japanese bank in London, citing ample Japanese demand.

By 1002 GMT the 30-year bond was quoted at 96-30, yielding 6.61 percent, compared with 96-17 in Tokyo and 96-20 in New York. The 10-year note had recovered to 98-13, yielding 6.34 percent, against 98-07 in New York.
Treasuries took a hit on Friday as investors' worries about renewed signs of inflation increased after a week of absorbing $38 billion worth of quarterly refunding.

The market's focus was firmly on the July retail sales data due out on Wednesday to gauge the level of economic activity, with possible effects on inflation. The consensus forecast was a rise of 0.7 percent on the headline figure, up from a 0.5 percent increase in the previous month.
"We are expecting a reasonable increase but nothing to really spook the market," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust in London.
Producer price inflation on Wednesday and consumer prices on Thursday will also fail to reveal any nasty surprises for investors, he said.
Traders said the market could do some more squaring up before entering the data.
"As important as the data is, we still need to correct some of the oversold situation from Friday before we can focus on positioning ourselves for that data," said the trader at the Japanese bank.

Economists said the bond market could ride out this week's welter of data without incurring further losses, but signs of a robust second half in the U.S. economy meant long term prospects were gloomy.
"We'll be in deep trouble if we get growth above three percent in the second half, which we think is quite a chance," said Amstad.
"So at some point the market will blow off," he said, but added for the time being Treasuries could just swing around, with investors adapting to the view that growth without inflation is a myth.
In the futures market, September T-bonds stood 9/32 up on the day at 112-31 in automated trade, after Friday's plunge from 114-10 at the open to a low of 112-08.
